*Generalizing Beyond the Regression Discontinuity Cutoff Using Panel Data: An Evaluation of Hybrid Tutoring*
(with Vivian Wong and Amy Dray)

## Abstract

Programs that assign services to students scoring below an eligibility threshold are usually evaluated with regression discontinuity designs. Those estimates are internally valid but apply only to students at the margin of eligibility, rarely the students furthest behind, whom such programs exist to serve. We develop and apply an estimand ladder that carries a causal estimate from the cutoff to the full assigned population, in an evaluation of Targeted Skills Instruction (TSI), a virtual tutoring program integrated with Edmentum's Exact Path personalized learning platform. Using a two-year panel of Renaissance Star reading and mathematics scores from a large urban district, we estimate four nested intent-to-treat effects of assignment: the level discontinuity at the cutoff from a sharp regression discontinuity; the growth discontinuity from a difference-in-discontinuities design that removes a pre-existing baseline gap; the effect for all assigned students from a two-period inverse probability-weighted difference-in-differences; and its six-period event-study extension. An exact algebraic bridge joins the second and third rungs: restricted to the RD bandwidth, the weighted difference-in-differences is identical to a sharp RD on the change score, so moving from the cutoff to the full population changes the sample, not the estimator. In reading, the effect generalizes and strengthens beyond the cutoff, from 0.11 standard deviations at the margin, to 0.18 under the aligned near-cutoff estimator, to 0.25 for the full assigned population, consistent with the program's targeting of students furthest behind. In mathematics, the ladder is diagnostic rather than confirmatory. The negative level discontinuity at the cutoff predates the intervention, and once that baseline gap is differenced out the cutoff benchmark is null. The full-population estimates are negative, but they rest on a single identification strategy, attenuate under alternative weighting, and are not corroborated by the null benchmark at the cutoff. We therefore read the mathematics evidence as ruling out benefit rather than demonstrating harm.
